For the last year, enterprise AI has been obsessed with taking humans out of the loop.
UiPath
made the opposite case: build better systems for humans and AI agents to work together.

But there’s a missing layer needed to make that collaboration work: context.

UiPath announced its approach:

🗺️ 𝗠𝗮𝗽 𝗼𝗳 𝗪𝗼𝗿𝗸
A living, governed definition of how work actually happens, including processes, rules, exceptions, systems, and human judgment.
🧭 𝗨𝗶𝗣𝗮𝘁𝗵 𝗖𝗮𝗿𝘁𝗼𝗴𝗿𝗮𝗽𝗵𝗲𝗿
Builds and maintains that Map from knowledge spread across documents, systems, and people, while humans approve what becomes part of it.
📚 𝗗𝗲𝗰𝗶𝘀𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗟𝗲𝗱𝗴𝗲𝗿
Captures decisions and exceptions as work happens, so new knowledge can be proposed back into the Map instead of getting lost.
🛤️ 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗿𝗮𝗶𝗹𝘀
Turn approved context into execution while keeping agents and workflows within defined boundaries.

The bigger shift is that context stops being something an agent simply retrieves at runtime and becomes part of the operating system of work itself.

The future of work isn’t just about giving agents more intelligence. 

It’s about giving humans and agents the shared context they need to work well together.

What does AI transformation look like when it’s working at scale?

The customer and partner panel at
UiPath
FUSION offered a far more compelling answer than any keynote slide.

A few moments stayed with me.
✅
SMBC Group
has automated the equivalent of 6 million hours of manual work, helping 3,000 people move into more strategic roles. In one month, its AI agent handled more than 10,000 employment-process requests and improved processing efficiency by 90%. Its CFO team shared an important lesson. Three process steps operating at 90% accuracy deliver only 73% end-to-end accuracy. That is why SMBC is redesigning processes around AI rather than adding AI to existing workflows. Kei Yamamoto calls it “AI by design".

✅
Nikki Harper
at
Mayo Clinic
,
Kevin Ireland
at
NatWest Group
,
Pramod Dibble
at
USAA
,
Timothy Garippa
at
Workday
, and others reinforced a consistent theme. Enterprise outcomes come from bringing together orchestration, automation, governance, and human oversight in one operating model.

✅
Diego Lo Giudice
at
Forrester
added another important dimension. Moving from deterministic software to AI agents changes how organizations test, govern, and build trust in technology.

Meaningful AI results depend on process context, governance, and the right human checkpoints along with powerful models.

After a decade working with clients on RPA and automation, hearing leaders share what is delivering value in production was the highlight of my week.

Stay tuned for my conversation with
Andrada Morar
, VP of Customer Experience and Global Partnerships at UiPath, on what it takes to orchestrate AI transformation across industries.

Is your AI agent creating value or creating activity you cannot govern?

That was the underlying tension at Day 2 of
UiPath
Fusion.
Kate Darling
challenged a familiar but limiting assumption. Stop comparing AI to humans. A better analogy is animals, partners with different capabilities, not substitutes for our own. We have always worked along with other forms of intelligence because their strengths complemented ours.

One unforgettable statistic. More than 85% of Roombas have names. We are wired to project agency and intent onto machines. That shapes how readily people overtrust, defer to, or excuse the failures of agentic systems. Design and governance must account for that.
UiPath
CMO
Michael Atalla
and CTO
Raghu Malpani
brought it to enterprise practice.
✅ Do not confuse autonomy with trust. Trust is earned through repeatable, observable performance.
✅ Start bounded. Read-only access, narrow tasks, human checkpoints before broader authority.
✅ Increase autonomy incrementally. Observe, validate, govern, then expand.
✅ Keep accountability human. AI proposes. Humans decide. Automation executes.

The real risk is not that AI moves too fast. It is that we automate in the wrong direction, optimizing for speed and cost while losing sight of people, purpose, and accountability.

What outcomes are we willing to delegate, and who remains accountable when those outcomes matter is the question every enterprise leader should ask.

Robots cannot perform the future. We do.
